screens.title: Structural Patterns — Facade and Proxy
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we study two complementary structural patterns that help manage complexity. First, the Facade pattern gives you one simple entry point to a collection of components so clients don’t need to learn internal sequences. Think of a single "Watch Movie" button that orchestrates TV, player, amplifier and speakers. Second, the Proxy pattern gives you a surrogate object that stands in for a real object and controls access to it — for example, to add lazy loading, security checks, logging, or caching. Both patterns reduce coupling, but they have different intents: Facade simplifies many objects as a unified A P I, while Proxy controls how and when a single object is accessed. You will see concrete Java examples: a ComputerFacade that sequences C P U, Memory and HardDrive calls, and an ImageProxy that performs permission checks and lazy loading. We will also implement a ReportingFacade and a Caching Proxy in guided exercises. By the end you should be able to pick the right pattern for simplifying subsystems or mediating access, understand common pitfalls, and apply these patterns in code. Which problem are you trying to solve — simplifying a workflow or controlling access — will determine which pattern to use.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives focus on understanding and implementing the core patterns. First, you will implement the Facade pattern to provide a simplified and unified interface to a complex subsystem. Second, you will identify scenarios where a Facade improves usability and reduces coupling, such as layered subsystems or complex startup sequences. You will learn to recognize smells that indicate a Facade will help, like clients that need to call several subsystem methods in a specific order. Finally on this screen you will see the importance of designing the Proxy and Real Subject to share an interface so they can be used interchangeably. screens.title: Facade Pattern: intent and analogy
screens.narratorSegment: The Facade pattern provides a single, unified interface to a set of interfaces in a subsystem. Concretely, a facade does not replace the subsystem classes; it delegates requests to them and hides the sequence and coordination required. The home theater analogy makes this clear: instead of toggling TV input, powering the amplifier, starting the DVD player and setting volume, you press one button that orchestrates all those commands. This reduces the cognitive load for the client and isolates changes inside the subsystem. A clear example is startup: clients call start() on a ComputerFacade, and the facade handles freeze, memory loading and C P U execution. A useful rule: a facade simplifies interactions and decouples clients from internal sequences, but should not contain substantive business logic of its own. Common misconceptions include thinking a facade should provide new complex behavior — instead it should primarily forward and orchestrate. When you design a facade, aim for a small set of meaningful operations that map to common client tasks. Think about layering: a facade can be the public A P I of a layer, shielding inner complexity and allowing the subsystem to evolve without breaking clients. What client task would you expose as a single facade method?

content.html:
Core Concept
Facade Pattern
A single, higher-level interface that delegates to multiple subsystem classes and hides complexity.
When to use
  • To reduce coupling between clients and a complex subsystem.
  • To provide a clear entry point to a layered subsystem.
  • To group common sequences into meaningful operations.
Common mistake
Avoid putting heavy business logic inside the façade; it should delegate work, not become the subsystem.
Key Takeaway

A facade simplifies access and reduces client dependency on internal sequences, making maintenance easier.

Analogy: Home Theater
TV: input and power
Amplifier: volume and source
DVD Player: load and play
Speakers: output
Facade action
One "Watch Movie" operation calls a sequence of subsystem methods to set power, inputs, and playback. The client does not need to know the order or parameters.
Concrete prompt
When many classes must be invoked in the correct order for a task, group that sequence into a facade method.

screens.title: When to apply a Facade
screens.narratorSegment: Recognizing when to use a Facade matters because it changes how components are organized and how clients interact. Use a facade when clients repeatedly call multiple subsystem methods in a specific sequence, when you need a stable public A P I for a subsystem, or when you want to decouple layers so the inner implementation can evolve independently. Typical design smells include duplicated sequences across clients, fragile client code that breaks when subsystem internals change, or a subsystem spread across many classes with no single entry point. When designing, prefer small, semantically meaningful facade methods that represent common tasks. For example, a computer startup is a single logical operation that requires a multi-step sequence: freeze the C P U, load memory from disk, jump to boot and execute. Wrapping those steps in start() protects clients from ordering requirements. A useful mental check: if a change in the subsystem would force multiple clients to change, a facade can reduce that ripple. Remember the caveat — don’t use a facade to hide poor design inside the subsystem. Use it to present a clear, stable interface and keep orchestration simple.

keyIdea.title: Design smells

content.html:
Process Flow
Apply a Facade
  1. 1. Identify repeated sequences where clients call multiple classes to complete a task.
  2. 2. Design a small set of high-level methods that represent common tasks.
  3. 3. Implement the facade to delegate and orchestrate subsystem calls in the correct order.
  4. 4. Keep business logic in subsystem classes; facade should mainly coordinate.
Key Takeaway

Use facade to stabilize an API for a complex subsystem so clients change less when internals evolve.

Example: Computer startup sequence
Clients must call freeze, load, jump, execute across CPU, Memory, and HardDrive. A ComputerFacade exposes start() and shutdown() so clients don’t need to perform each step.
Why it matters
It reduces coupling, centralizes coordination, and makes the subsystem easier to test and maintain because the orchestration sequence lives in one place.
Misconception check
A facade is not a substitute for sound subsystem design — it hides complexity but does not fix poor internal cohesion.

screens.title: ComputerFacade — Java demo
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the ComputerFacade example step by step. The system has three subsystem classes: C P U with freeze, jump and execute; Memory with load; and HardDrive with read. Without a facade, a client would need to know the exact sequence: freeze the processor, load memory with boot sector read from disk, jump to start and execute. The ComputerFacade constructor creates subsystem instances and exposes start() and shutdown() methods. In start(), the facade logs startup, calls processor. freeze(), calls R A M. load(0, hd. read(0, 1024)) to load the boot sector, then processor. jump(0) and processor. execute(). This sequence is the coordination responsibility of the facade. The client code simply constructs a ComputerFacade and calls start() and shutdown(), freeing client code from ordering concerns. The practical benefit is reduced coupling and easier maintenance: changes inside C P U, Memory or HardDrive rarely require client updates. A common mistake is adding heavy business logic inside start() — keep orchestration thin and let subsystems perform domain work. Try to name facade methods by high-level tasks that clients understand. ComputerFacade — Java demo means the computerfacade sequences subsystem calls so clients use a single start() instead of multiple coordinated calls.. In practical terms, a concise startup/shutdown facade that orchestrates cpu, memory and harddrive. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Facade orchestration
keyIdea.text: The ComputerFacade sequences subsystem calls so clients use a single start() instead of multiple coordinated calls.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
ComputerFacade (Java)
The facade constructs subsystem objects and exposes a start method that sequences calls.
// Subsystems
class CPU {
  public void freeze() { System.out.println("CPU: Freezing..."); }
  public void jump(long position) { System.out.println("CPU: Jumping to " + position + "..."); }
  public void execute() { System.out.println("CPU: Executing commands..."); }
}

class Memory {
  public void load(long position, byte[] data) {
    System.out.println("Memory: Loading data to " + position + "...");
  }
}

class HardDrive {
  public byte[] read(long lba, int size) {
    System.out.println("HardDrive: Reading " + size + " bytes from LBA " + lba + "...");
    return new byte[]{'b','o','o','t'}; // Simulate boot sector
  }
}

// Facade
class ComputerFacade {
  private CPU processor;
  private Memory ram;
  private HardDrive hd;

  public ComputerFacade() {
    this.processor = new CPU();
    this.ram = new Memory();
    this.hd = new HardDrive();
  }

  public void start() {
    System.out.println("\
Computer starting up...");
    processor.freeze();
    ram.load(0, hd.read(0, 1024));
    processor.jump(0);
    processor.execute();
    System.out.println("Computer startup complete.\
");
  }

  public void shutdown() {
    System.out.println("\
Computer shutting down...");
    System.out.println("Saving state...");
    System.out.println("Powering off components...");
    System.out.println("Computer shut down.\
");
  }
}

// Client
public class User {
  public static void main(String[] args) {
    ComputerFacade computer = new ComputerFacade();
    computer.start();
    computer.shutdown();
  }
}
Example output
CPU: Freezing... Memory: Loading data to 0... HardDrive: Reading 1024 bytes... CPU: Jumping to 0... CPU: Executing commands...
Pro tip
Keep the facade focused on orchestration and name methods by the task the client wants to perform.
Explanation
The facade reduces client knowledge: clients do not need to know how to read boot sector or which load parameters to pass. It centralizes sequence management in one place for maintainability and testability.
Check your understanding
If a subsystem method signature changes, only the facade should need updates, not every client that used the old sequence.

screens.title: Proxy Pattern: intent and metaphor
screens.narratorSegment: The Proxy pattern provides a surrogate or placeholder for another object to control access to it. The proxy implements the same interface as the real subject and can run logic before or after delegating requests. Think of a security guard at a vault: the guard checks credentials, denies entry to unauthorized users, and allows access to permitted users. Proxies solve problems such as lazy initialization (virtual proxy), permission checks (protection proxy), representing remote resources locally (remote proxy), logging requests, or caching results. The key is that the proxy and real subject share an interface, so clients remain unchanged while access policies or optimizations are applied. A common pitfall is confusing proxies with decorators; unlike a decorator, a proxy’s primary role is controlling access and possibly delaying or routing calls, not adding responsibilities to the object’s behavior. When designing a proxy, choose clear access policies, and be mindful of side effects such as added latency or complexity. Ask yourself whether you need control over creation, access, or location — that will drive the proxy design. Proxy Pattern: intent and metaphor means implement the same interface as the real subject and add access control, lazy loading, remote stubs, logging, or caching behavior.. In practical terms, a surrogate that controls access to a real object. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Core Concept
Proxy Pattern
A proxy stands in for the real subject, controlling access and potentially performing lazy creation, protection, logging, remote marshalling, or caching.
Virtual: lazy creation
Protection: permission checks
Remote: local stub for remote object
Caching: store results
Metaphor: Security Guard
A guard checks credentials before admitting someone to a vault; similarly, a protection proxy verifies access before invoking methods on a sensitive object.
Design note
Make sure the proxy and real subject share an interface so substitution is transparent to clients. Keep access policies simple and visible.
Key Takeaway

Proxies add a control layer around an object without changing its interface, enabling lazy loading, protection, remote access, logging, or caching.

screens.title: ImageProxy — protection and lazy loading
screens.narratorSegment: Let's examine the ImageProxy example that combines protection and virtual proxy behavior. The subject interface Image declares display(). RealImage is the heavy object that loads the file from disk in its constructor by calling loadFromDisk, which simulates a delay. ImageProxy holds a filename, a boolean isAdmin, and a reference to RealImage. On display(), ImageProxy first checks permission: if the caller is not an admin, it prints an access denied message and never creates the heavy object. If the caller is an admin and the real image reference is null, the proxy creates RealImage, which triggers the expensive load. On subsequent display() calls, the real image is already loaded and display() is delegated directly. This example demonstrates two common proxy responsibilities: protection based on roles and lazy initialization to avoid expensive construction until necessary. A lesson here is to separate access checks from object creation carefully so you don't prematurely instantiate heavy objects for unauthorized users. Also, prefer caching the loaded instance if repeated accesses are expected. ImageProxy — protection and lazy loading means an imageproxy can both prevent unauthorized access and defer expensive creation until it is necessary (lazy loading).. In practical terms, a java proxy that enforces permissions and performs lazy load. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
ImageProxy (Java)
Proxy implements the same Image interface and controls loading and access.
// Subject Interface
interface Image {
  void display();
}

// Real Subject
class RealImage implements Image {
  private String filename;

  public RealImage(String filename) {
    this.filename = filename;
    loadFromDisk(filename); // Expensive
  }

  private void loadFromDisk(String filename) {
    System.out.println("Loading " + filename + " from disk...");
    try { Thread.sleep(2000); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
  }

  @Override
  public void display() {
    System.out.println("Displaying " + filename);
  }
}

// Proxy
class ImageProxy implements Image {
  private RealImage realImage;
  private String filename;
  private boolean isAdmin;

  public ImageProxy(String filename, boolean isAdmin) {
    this.filename = filename;
    this.isAdmin = isAdmin;
  }

  @Override
  public void display() {
    if (isAdmin) {
      if (realImage == null) { realImage = new RealImage(filename); }
      realImage.display();
    } else {
      System.out.println("Access Denied: You must be an admin to display " + filename);
    }
  }
}
Observed behavior
Admin call: triggers load then display. Guest call: prints access denied and does not load file.
Pro tip
Combine protection and virtual behavior carefully: check permissions before instantiation to avoid wasted work.
Sequence diagram (conceptual)
Client → Proxy: display() → Proxy checks isAdmin → if allowed, Proxy creates RealImage if null → Proxy delegates display() to RealImage.
Check your understanding
How would you change the proxy to cache thumbnails separately from full images? Consider adding a lightweight thumbnail path and only loading the full image when needed.

screens.title: Facade vs Proxy
screens.narratorSegment: Facade and Proxy can look similar because both wrap other objects, but their intents differ and that guides their proper use. A Facade provides a simplified interface over a group of classes — its goal is usability and decoupling of clients from subsystem sequences. Its scope is a subsystem or a layer. A Proxy provides controlled access to a single object and its responsibilities often include lazy creation, permission checks, caching, or acting as a local representative for a remote object. Scope for a proxy is generally one subject. A common confusion is thinking both are interchangeable; they are not. If you need to hide many object interactions behind one A P I, choose Facade. If you need to control how or when an individual object is accessed, use Proxy. Another confusion is with Decorator: Decorator adds responsibilities to an object, while Proxy controls access without changing the underlying contract. When in doubt, ask: am I simplifying many collaborators, or mediating access to one? That question points to Facade or Proxy respectively. Facade vs Proxy means facade simplifies many objects into one api; proxy mediates access to a single object for control or optimization.. In practical terms, clarifying intent, scope, and common confusions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

narration.text: Facade and Proxy can look similar because both wrap other objects, but their intents differ and that guides their proper use. A Facade provides a simplified interface over a group of classes — its goal is usability and decoupling of clients from subsystem sequences. Its scope is a subsystem or a layer. A Proxy provides controlled access to a single object and its responsibilities often include lazy creation, permission checks, caching, or acting as a local representative for a remote object. Scope for a proxy is generally one subject. A common confusion is thinking both are interchangeable; they are not. If you need to hide many object interactions behind one A P I, choose Facade. If you need to control how or when an individual object is accessed, use Proxy. Another confusion is with Decorator: Decorator adds responsibilities to an object, while Proxy controls access without changing the underlying contract. When in doubt, ask: am I simplifying many collaborators, or mediating access to one? That question points to Facade or Proxy respectively. Facade vs Proxy means facade simplifies many objects into one api; proxy mediates access to a single object for control or optimization.. In practical terms, clarifying intent, scope, and common confusions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Intent differs
keyIdea.text: Facade simplifies many objects into one API; Proxy mediates access to a single object for control or optimization.

content.html:
Comparison
Facade
  • Intent: Simplify a subsystem.
  • Scope: Group of classes or a layer.
  • When: Repeated sequences, create a stable API.
Comparison
Proxy
  • Intent: Control access or optimize a single object.
  • Scope: One subject instance.
  • When: Lazy load, protect resources, cache results, or present remote objects locally.
Misconception check
Do not use a facade to hide poor internal design, and do not use a proxy to add unrelated behaviors — each pattern has a focused intent.
Facade = simplify many
Proxy = control or optimize one
Decorator ≠ Proxy: decorator adds behavior

Starter Code
ReportingFacade
Implement generateDailyReport to orchestrate data fetch, formatting and export.
// Subsystem Components
class ReportDataFetcher {
  public String fetchData(String query) {

    System.out.println("Exporting '" + formattedReport + "' to " + destination);
  }
}

// TODO: Implement ReportingFacade that uses the three components

Fetching data → Formatting → Exporting. The facade centralizes this sequence into a single method call for the client.

Keep the facade thin: pass parameters through to subsystems, log meaningful messages, and let subsystems hold heavy behavior like formatting and exporting.

screens.title: Task 2 — DataServiceProxy (caching)
screens.narratorSegment: The DataServiceProxy task asks you to implement a proxy that caches results to avoid repeated heavy calls. The subject interface DataService declares getData(key). HeavyDataService simulates a slow remote call by sleeping and returning data for a key. DataServiceProxy should maintain a cache map keyed by request keys. On getData(key), if the cache contains the value return it and log a cache hit. If not, call the real service, store the result in the cache and return it, logging a cache miss. This proxy implements the caching proxy role and preserves the DataService interface so clients are unaffected. The hands-on value here is seeing dramatic differences in console traces: first call shows a heavy fetch, second call for the same key prints a cache hit and returns immediately. Consider cache eviction policies for real systems, but for the exercise a simple in-memory map demonstrates the pattern. This exercise builds intuition about trade-offs: caching improves latency but adds complexity and memory use. keyIdea.text: Use a proxy to cache expensive results by key so subsequent calls return quickly without contacting the real service.

content.html:
Starter Code
DataServiceProxy
Implement caching in the proxy so repeated keys return cached values.
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

// Subject Interface
interface DataService {
  String getData(String key);
}

// Real Subject
class HeavyDataService implements DataService {
  @Override
  public String getData(String key) {
    System.out.println("HeavyDataService: Fetching data for key '" + key + "' from remote source...");
    try { Thread.sleep(2000); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
    return "Data for " + key + " (from real service)";
  }
}

// TODO: Implement DataServiceProxy that caches results

First call: cache miss and heavy fetch. Second call: cache hit and immediate return.
Design note
In production consider expiration, size limits, and thread safety for caches. For the exercise a simple map is sufficient.
Client sample
DataService service = new DataServiceProxy(); service.getData("reportA"); service.getData("reportA");
Check your understanding
Observe how the proxy reduces repeated heavy fetches and think about the trade-offs around memory and stale data.

screens.title: Trade-offs and benefits
screens.narratorSegment: Using Facade and Proxy brings clear benefits but also trade-offs to consider. Benefits include reduced client complexity, clearer public APIs, and the ability to centralize coordination or access policies. For facades this reduces coupling and simplifies client code; for proxies it enables lazy loading, protection and caching without changing client code. Trade-offs include added indirection: facades can become catch-alls if you add too much logic, and proxies can introduce latency or hide costly operations. Also, proxies add another object lifecycle to manage and may complicate debugging because calls are rerouted through the proxy. Design recommendations: keep facade methods small and descriptive, let subsystems contain business logic, and log actions inside proxies so expensive or blocked operations are visible. For caching proxies, plan eviction and consistency strategies. Finally, monitor the system for performance or maintenance pain; if a pattern creates more confusion than simplification, revisit the design. The core idea is to use these patterns deliberately to clarify intent, not to conceal complexity. Trade-offs and benefits means apply patterns deliberately: prefer clarity and stable apis for facades, and transparent, observable proxies for access and optimization.. In practical terms, when these patterns help, and what you should watch out for. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Apply patterns deliberately: prefer clarity and stable APIs for facades, and transparent, observable proxies for access and optimization.

content.html:
Architecture
Benefits and trade-offs
Benefits
  • Reduces coupling and simplifies client code (Facade).
  • Enables lazy creation, protection and caching without client changes (Proxy).
  • Centralizes coordination and access policies for easier maintenance.
Trade-offs
  • Added indirection can hide costs or complicate debugging.
  • Facades can become overloaded with logic if abused.
  • Caching proxies require eviction and consistency strategies.
Best practices
  1. Keep facade methods focused on client tasks.
  2. Separate access checks from heavy instantiation in proxies.
  3. Log proxy decisions to make hidden behavior visible.
Key Takeaway

Use these patterns to express intent: simplify or mediate. Avoid hiding important behavior without visibility and controls.

Pattern selection practice
Analyze the scenario, name the primary problem and pick Facade or Proxy with justification.
Scenario 1
A TradingEngine requires order, risk checks and market data to execute a trade. Which pattern?

screens.title: Terminal traces: why console output matters

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we study two complementary structural patterns that help manage complexity. First, the Facade pattern gives you one simple entry point to a collection of components so clients don’t need to learn internal sequences. Think of a single "Watch Movie" button that orchestrates TV, player, amplifier and speakers. Second, the Proxy pattern gives you a surrogate object that stands in for a real object and controls access to it — for example, to add lazy loading, security checks, logging, or caching. Both patterns reduce coupling, but they have different intents: Facade simplifies many objects as a unified A P I, while Proxy controls how and when a single object is accessed. You will see concrete Java examples: a ComputerFacade that sequences C P U, Memory and HardDrive calls, and an ImageProxy that performs permission checks and lazy loading. We will also implement a ReportingFacade and a Caching Proxy in guided exercises. By the end you should be able to pick the right pattern for simplifying subsystems or mediating access, understand common pitfalls, and apply these patterns in code. Which problem are you trying to solve — simplifying a workflow or controlling access — will determine which pattern to use.

These objectives focus on understanding and implementing the core patterns. First, you will implement the Facade pattern to provide a simplified and unified interface to a complex subsystem. Practically, that means writing a small class that orchestrates sequence and coordination so clients call one method instead of many. Second, you will identify scenarios where a Facade improves usability and reduces coupling, such as layered subsystems or complex startup sequences. You will learn to recognize smells that indicate a Facade will help, like clients that need to call several subsystem methods in a specific order. Third, you will implement a Proxy to provide a surrogate or placeholder for another object; this includes adding logic for access control or lazy initialization. Finally on this screen you will see the importance of designing the Proxy and Real Subject to share an interface so they can be used interchangeably. Each objective includes a short explanation and a mnemonic to help you remember when to apply the pattern.

These objectives focus on types of proxy, analysis and practical application. You will distinguish between proxy types — virtual for lazy creation, protection for permission checks, remote for local stubs to remote objects, logging for request auditing, and caching proxies to avoid repeated heavy operations. This distinction matters because each proxy type solves a different problem even though they share the same structural form. Next you will analyze trade-offs and benefits for using Facade and Proxy. For example, a Facade reduces coupling but should not become a place for heavy business logic; a Proxy adds a control layer but can introduce latency or single points of failure. Finally, you will apply the patterns in guided tasks: create a ReportingFacade to generate and export reports, and implement a caching DataServiceProxy to save expensive retrievals. These practice tasks cement patterns by making the consequences of design choices visible in console traces and code structure.

The Facade pattern provides a single, unified interface to a set of interfaces in a subsystem. Concretely, a facade does not replace the subsystem classes; it delegates requests to them and hides the sequence and coordination required. The home theater analogy makes this clear: instead of toggling TV input, powering the amplifier, starting the DVD player and setting volume, you press one button that orchestrates all those commands. This reduces the cognitive load for the client and isolates changes inside the subsystem. A clear example is startup: clients call start() on a ComputerFacade, and the facade handles freeze, memory loading and C P U execution. A useful rule: a facade simplifies interactions and decouples clients from internal sequences, but should not contain substantive business logic of its own. Common misconceptions include thinking a facade should provide new complex behavior — instead it should primarily forward and orchestrate. When you design a facade, aim for a small set of meaningful operations that map to common client tasks. Think about layering: a facade can be the public A P I of a layer, shielding inner complexity and allowing the subsystem to evolve without breaking clients. What client task would you expose as a single facade method?

Recognizing when to use a Facade matters because it changes how components are organized and how clients interact. Use a facade when clients repeatedly call multiple subsystem methods in a specific sequence, when you need a stable public A P I for a subsystem, or when you want to decouple layers so the inner implementation can evolve independently. Typical design smells include duplicated sequences across clients, fragile client code that breaks when subsystem internals change, or a subsystem spread across many classes with no single entry point. When designing, prefer small, semantically meaningful facade methods that represent common tasks. For example, a computer startup is a single logical operation that requires a multi-step sequence: freeze the C P U, load memory from disk, jump to boot and execute. Wrapping those steps in start() protects clients from ordering requirements. A useful mental check: if a change in the subsystem would force multiple clients to change, a facade can reduce that ripple. Remember the caveat — don’t use a facade to hide poor design inside the subsystem. Use it to present a clear, stable interface and keep orchestration simple.

Let's walk through the ComputerFacade example step by step. The system has three subsystem classes: C P U with freeze, jump and execute; Memory with load; and HardDrive with read. The Proxy pattern provides a surrogate or placeholder for another object to control access to it. The proxy implements the same interface as the real subject and can run logic before or after delegating requests. Think of a security guard at a vault: the guard checks credentials, denies entry to unauthorized users, and allows access to permitted users. Proxies solve problems such as lazy initialization (virtual proxy), permission checks (protection proxy), representing remote resources locally (remote proxy), logging requests, or caching results. The key is that the proxy and real subject share an interface, so clients remain unchanged while access policies or optimizations are applied. A common pitfall is confusing proxies with decorators; unlike a decorator, a proxy’s primary role is controlling access and possibly delaying or routing calls, not adding responsibilities to the object’s behavior. When designing a proxy, choose clear access policies, and be mindful of side effects such as added latency or complexity. Ask yourself whether you need control over creation, access, or location — that will drive the proxy design. In practical terms, a surrogate that controls access to a real object. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Let's examine the ImageProxy example that combines protection and virtual proxy behavior. The subject interface Image declares display(). RealImage is the heavy object that loads the file from disk in its constructor by calling loadFromDisk, which simulates a delay. ImageProxy holds a filename, a boolean isAdmin, and a reference to RealImage. On display(), ImageProxy first checks permission: if the caller is not an admin, it prints an access denied message and never creates the heavy object. If the caller is an admin and the real image reference is null, the proxy creates RealImage, which triggers the expensive load. On subsequent display() calls, the real image is already loaded and display() is delegated directly. This example demonstrates two common proxy responsibilities: protection based on roles and lazy initialization to avoid expensive construction until necessary. A lesson here is to separate access checks from object creation carefully so you don't prematurely instantiate heavy objects for unauthorized users. Also, prefer caching the loaded instance if repeated accesses are expected. Facade and Proxy can look similar because both wrap other objects, but their intents differ and that guides their proper use. A Facade provides a simplified interface over a group of classes — its goal is usability and decoupling of clients from subsystem sequences. Its scope is a subsystem or a layer. A Proxy provides controlled access to a single object and its responsibilities often include lazy creation, permission checks, caching, or acting as a local representative for a remote object. Scope for a proxy is generally one subject. A common confusion is thinking both are interchangeable; they are not. If you need to hide many object interactions behind one A P I, choose Facade. If you need to control how or when an individual object is accessed, use Proxy. Another confusion is with Decorator: Decorator adds responsibilities to an object, while Proxy controls access without changing the underlying contract. When in doubt, ask: am I simplifying many collaborators, or mediating access to one? That question points to Facade or Proxy respectively. Facade vs Proxy means facade simplifies many objects into one api; proxy mediates access to a single object for control or optimization.. Using Facade and Proxy brings clear benefits but also trade-offs to consider. Benefits include reduced client complexity, clearer public APIs, and the ability to centralize coordination or access policies. For facades this reduces coupling and simplifies client code; for proxies it enables lazy loading, protection and caching without changing client code. Trade-offs include added indirection: facades can become catch-alls if you add too much logic, and proxies can introduce latency or hide costly operations. Also, proxies add another object lifecycle to manage and may complicate debugging because calls are rerouted through the proxy. Design recommendations: keep facade methods small and descriptive, let subsystems contain business logic, and log actions inside proxies so expensive or blocked operations are visible. For caching proxies, plan eviction and consistency strategies. Finally, monitor the system for performance or maintenance pain; if a pattern creates more confusion than simplification, revisit the design. The core idea is to use these patterns deliberately to clarify intent, not to conceal complexity. Here are the central concepts to retain. The Facade Pattern offers a unified, higher-level interface that simplifies a subsystem by orchestrating multiple objects and hiding sequence details. A Subsystem is the collection of related classes that perform a complex task and which the facade shields clients from. The Proxy Pattern provides a surrogate or placeholder for a real object, enabling access control, lazy loading, logging, caching, or remote representation. Keep these definitions in mind as you inspect code: if multiple classes must be called in order, consider a facade; if you need to control creation or access to a single object, consider a proxy. Use console traces to observe when heavy work occurs and prefer small, purpose-named facade methods. Remember that misapplying either pattern can hide complexity or introduce unnecessary indirection, so choose deliberately.

A few compact reminders will help as you apply these patterns. Subject is the interface both a proxy and a real subject implement. Real Subject is the actual object providing core functionality. Lazy Loading is an optimization where objects are created only when first needed; virtual proxy commonly implements this. Protection proxies enforce permission checks and prevent unauthorized access. When you design, prefer clear naming, keep orchestration in facades, and keep access checks and instantiation rules explicit in proxies.
